description: Team AsaneCrown leverages NASA Earth observation data & AI for environmental solutions.
summary:
The Dhemaji Flood Recovery and Reconstruction Intelligence System is a web-based platform that helps identify flood-affected areas and plan recovery using satellite data.
The system uses NASA-ISRO NISAR radar images to detect possible changes in floodwater, even when clouds make it difficult for regular satellites to observe the ground. It combines this information with OpenStreetMap and WorldPop data to estimate the impact on buildings, roads, facilities, and nearby populations.

Based on the analysis, the system identifies potentially affected infrastructure, ranks recovery priorities into three levels (P1, P2, and P3), and suggests routes for recovery teams.
Through an interactive dashboard, users can view satellite comparisons, flood maps, affected infrastructure, population estimates, and recovery plans in one place.
The goal is to help disaster management authorities understand flood impacts, prioritize important repairs, and make faster, more informed recovery decisions.
details:
1. Project Overview

The Dhemaji Flood Recovery and Reconstruction Intelligence System is a geospatial decision-support platform developed to help identify potential flood impacts and support infrastructure recovery planning in Dhemaji, Assam, India. Instead of simply displaying flood maps, the system transforms satellite observations into useful information for identifying affected areas, assessing infrastructure impacts, and prioritizing recovery activities.

2. How Does It Work?

The system uses real NASA-ISRO NISAR L-band Synthetic Aperture Radar (SAR) data. Unlike conventional optical satellite imagery, radar can observe the Earth's surface through cloud cover and during nighttime.

The processing workflow includes:

  1. Satellite Data Collection: Acquiring NISAR L2 GCOV radar observations from different dates through NASA's Alaska Satellite Facility (ASF DAAC).
  2. Data Preprocessing: Preparing radar images through cropping, common-grid alignment, conversion to decibels (dB), and noise filtering.
  3. Floodwater Analysis: Comparing radar observations to identify candidate floodwater changes while accounting for permanent water bodies.
  4. Infrastructure Assessment: Combining the results with OpenStreetMap data to examine potentially affected buildings, roads, and essential facilities.
  5. Population Assessment: Using WorldPop 2020 population data to estimate the population potentially affected.
  6. Recovery Prioritization: Applying a weighted scoring approach to rank potentially affected assets into three priority levels: P1, P2, and P3.
  7. Recovery Route Planning: Generating suggested routes to support recovery teams in accessing important locations.
  8. Interactive Dashboard: Presenting satellite comparisons, flood-related map layers, infrastructure impacts, and recovery priorities through a web-based interface.

3. Key Benefits and Features

  • Identifies potential floodwater changes using satellite radar observations.
  • Supports flood monitoring even under cloud-covered conditions.
  • Provides satellite image comparisons across different observation dates.
  • Estimates potential impacts on buildings, roads, facilities, and populations.
  • Highlights potentially affected and inaccessible road segments.
  • Organizes infrastructure recovery priorities.
  • Provides suggested recovery routes for planning.
  • Combines multiple geospatial datasets in one interactive dashboard.
  • Supports more transparent and data-driven recovery decisions.

4. Innovation and Creativity

The main innovation is connecting satellite-based flood detection with infrastructure impact assessment and reconstruction planning in a single platform. Traditional flood maps primarily show where water is present, whereas our system takes the next step by examining what infrastructure may be affected, estimating nearby population impacts, ranking recovery priorities, and suggesting possible routes.

The integration of NISAR radar observations, GIS analysis, population data, infrastructure mapping, and route planning creates a practical approach to transforming Earth observation data into actionable recovery intelligence.

5. Tools, Technologies, and Resources

Satellite and Geospatial Data:

  • NASA-ISRO NISAR L2 GCOV and GOFF products.
  • OpenStreetMap infrastructure data.
  • WorldPop 2020 population data.

Programming Languages:

  • Python 3.13
  • JavaScript / JSX

Backend and Data Processing:

  • FastAPI
  • Rasterio
  • GeoPandas
  • Shapely
  • NumPy
  • SciPy
  • OpenCV
  • NetworkX
  • h5py
  • pyproj

Frontend and Visualization:

  • React 18
  • Leaflet 1.9
  • Chart.js 4
  • Vite 5

Development and GIS Tools:

  • ASF Vertex and asf_search
  • QGIS
  • Visual Studio Code
  • Git

Hardware: Standard laptops were used for development and data processing. No specialized hardware was required.

6. Intended Impact

The project aims to support disaster management authorities, local administrations, and recovery planners by providing accessible information about potential flood impacts and infrastructure priorities.

It has the potential to:

  • Improve awareness of flood-affected locations.
  • Help prioritize critical infrastructure repairs.
  • Support better allocation of recovery resources.
  • Identify possible road accessibility challenges.
  • Assist recovery teams in planning their activities.
  • Extend satellite-based recovery analysis to other flood-prone regions.

7. Factors Considered and Limitations

During development, we considered satellite data availability, spatial resolution, cloud cover, permanent water bodies, population distribution, infrastructure coverage, road accessibility, and the reliability of geospatial estimates.

The analysis uses approximately 10–20 m pixel estimates and does not represent a building-level damage survey. Wet agricultural fields may resemble water, and flooded vegetation can produce different radar responses. Detection thresholds were locally tuned, and the results require ground validation using field observations and official flood reports.

We also considered the importance of transparent results, accessible visualizations, open data resources, and the ability to update the analysis with additional satellite observations.

Our ultimate goal is to bridge the gap between satellite-based flood monitoring and practical recovery planning, turning space-based intelligence into meaningful decisions that can help communities recover and become more resilient.
